Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ClickFix Campaigns Expand Malware Delivery With New Loaders and Fake Update Lures

The Hacker News
2026-06-16 18 use cases 9 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged multiple ClickFix campaigns that deliver three malware loaders called BabaDeda Loader, Lorem Ipsum Loader, and Potemkin, per independent reports from Morphisec, BlueVoyant, and Huntress, respectively. Attacks involving BabaDeda Loader, observed in April 2026, have targeted education and financial organizations. "Earlier BabaDeda activity was known for

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ClickFix Run-dialog PowerShell download chain (BabaDeda/Lorem Ipsum/Potemkin) · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] MSI installer spawning HTA payload (Potemkin delivery chain) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ClickFix Campaigns Expand Malware Delivery With New Loaders and Fake Update Lure
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Outdated Node.js v7.10.1 launched from user-writable path (Lorem Ipsum Loader) · [LLM] DLL side-load of mscoree.dll or msvcp140.dll from non-System32 path (Lorem Ipsum) · [LLM] Potemkin host-marker file %LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver creation · [LLM] Storage Crypter external-storage payload read (BabaDeda List.Control.dat) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
ClickFix Run-dialog PowerShell download chain (BabaDeda/Lorem Ipsum/Potemkin) AIDelivery Medium
Detects the ClickFix social-engineering entry point common to all three loader families: explorer.exe (Run dialog paste) spawning a hidden PowerShell that immediately downloads a ZIP, Node.js binary, MSI, or .dat staging payload. This pivots on parent=explorer because ClickFix tricks the user into pasting the attacker-supplied command into Win+R. Rationale: Article describes all three loader families (BabaDeda, Lorem Ipsum, Potemkin) using ClickFix to coerce users into pasting attacker-supplied PowerShell into the Run dialog — making parent=explorer.exe the strongest behavioural anchor. Cmdline tokens (Node.js, ZIP, MSI, HTA, .dat) match the staged delivery shapes described per family.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin pasting a winget/Chocolatey bootstrap into Win+R
  • Software deployment teams running adhoc PS one-liners that fetch internal MSIs
  • Developer test scripts launched manually from Run dialog with Invoke-WebRequest
  • Endpoint health-check scripts pushed via vendor docs ("paste this in Run")
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "winget" and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("winget", "chocolatey", "choco install", "\\\\corp.local\\", "\\\\internal.")
Response runbook
Triage: Pull the full PS cmdline plus 5-minute child-process tail on the same host — look for node.exe, msiexec.exe, mshta.exe, or DLL side-load follow-ons. Resolve any URL in the cmdline against VT/URLhaus and check whether the host is education/finance (BabaDeda target sector) or recently visited a compromised WordPress site. Contain: Isolate the device via Defender Live Response if any follow-on stage 2 (Node.js from user path, mshta, rundll32 of side-loaded DLL) fired; kill the PS process tree; revoke recent user tokens. Hunt: Pivot on the user across the prior 24h for SEO-driven downloads, Edge "security update" lures in browser history, and other hosts that contacted the same C2 URL.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-w hidden", "-windowstyle hidden", "-WindowStyle h", "-nop", "-noprofile")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("DownloadFile", "Invoke-WebRequest", "iwr ", "Invoke-RestMethod", "irm ", "Invoke-Expression", "iex ", "curl ", "Start-BitsTransfer")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".zip", "node", ".msi", ".dat", "mshta", ".hta")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\explorer.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("-w hidden", "-windowstyle hidden", "-WindowStyle h", "-nop", "-noprofile")
| where CommandLine has_any ("DownloadFile", "Invoke-WebRequest", "iwr ", "Invoke-RestMethod", "irm ", "Invoke-Expression", "iex ", "curl ", "Start-BitsTransfer")
| where CommandLine has_any (".zip", "node", ".msi", ".dat", "mshta", ".hta")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ClickFix Run-Dialog PowerShell Download Chain
id: 7f3e2a1b-9c4d-4e8a-b6f2-1d3c5e7a9b21
status: experimental
description: PowerShell launched from explorer.exe (Win+R Run-dialog paste) with a hidden window flag and an inline download cmdlet pulling a ZIP, Node.js, MSI, or .dat payload — the canonical ClickFix entry point used to drop BabaDeda, Lorem Ipsum, and Potemkin loaders.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/clickfix-campaigns-expand-malware.html
author: SOC Detection Team
date: 2026/06/17
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1566.002
  - attack.t1204.001
  - attack.t1059.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\explorer.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
  selection_window:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '-w hidden'
      - '-windowstyle hidden'
      - '-WindowStyle h'
      - '-nop'
      - '-noprofile'
  selection_download:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'DownloadFile'
      - 'Invoke-WebRequest'
      - 'iwr '
      - 'Invoke-RestMethod'
      - 'irm '
      - 'Invoke-Expression'
      - 'iex '
      - 'Start-BitsTransfer'
  selection_payload:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '.zip'
      - 'node'
      - '.msi'
      - '.dat'
      - 'mshta'
      - '.hta'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_window and selection_download and selection_payload
falsepositives:
  - IT admin Win+R PowerShell one-liners that download internal tooling
  - Software-deployment scripts run interactively from Run dialog
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\explorer.exe OR *\\Explorer.EXE OR *\\EXPLORER.EXE) @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe) (@CommandLine:*hidden* OR @CommandLine:*-nop* OR @CommandLine:*-noprofile*) (@CommandLine:*DownloadFile* OR @CommandLine:*Invoke-WebRequest* OR @CommandLine:*iwr* OR @CommandLine:*Invoke-RestMethod* OR @CommandLine:*irm* OR @CommandLine:*Invoke-Expression* OR @CommandLine:*iex* OR @CommandLine:*Start-BitsTransfer*) (@CommandLine:*.zip* OR @CommandLine:*node* OR @CommandLine:*.msi* OR @CommandLine:*.dat* OR @CommandLine:*mshta* OR @CommandLine:*.hta*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/explorer\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/(?i)(-w\s+hidden|-windowstyle\s+hidden|-WindowStyle\s+h|-nop|-noprofile)/
| CommandLine=/(?i)(DownloadFile|Invoke-WebRequest|iwr\s|Invoke-RestMethod|irm\s|Invoke-Expression|iex\s|Start-BitsTransfer|curl\s)/
| CommandLine=/(?i)(\.zip|node|\.msi|\.dat|mshta|\.hta)/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime FROM datamodel=Endpoint.Processes WHERE Processes.parent_process_name=explorer.exe AND Processes.process_name IN (powershell.exe, pwsh.exe) AND (Processes.process="*hidden*" OR Processes.process="* -nop *" OR Processes.process="*-windowstyle h*") AND (Processes.process="*DownloadFile*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-WebRequest*" OR Processes.process="*iwr *" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-RestMethod*" OR Processes.process="*irm *" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*" OR Processes.process="*iex *" OR Processes.process="*curl *") AND (Processes.process="*.zip*" OR Processes.process="*node*" OR Processes.process="*.msi*" OR Processes.process="*.dat*" OR Processes.process="*mshta*") BY Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime FROM datamodel=Endpoint.Processes WHERE Processes.parent_process_name=explorer.exe AND Processes.process_name IN (powershell.exe, pwsh.exe) AND (Processes.process="*hidden*" OR Processes.process="* -nop *" OR Processes.process="*-windowstyle h*") AND (Processes.process="*DownloadFile*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-WebRequest*" OR Processes.process="*iwr *" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-RestMethod*" OR Processes.process="*irm *" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*" OR Processes.process="*iex *" OR Processes.process="*curl *") AND (Processes.process="*.zip*" OR Processes.process="*node*" OR Processes.process="*.msi*" OR Processes.process="*.dat*" OR Processes.process="*mshta*") BY Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Outdated Node.js v7.10.1 launched from user-writable path (Lorem Ipsum Loader) AIInstallation High
Lorem Ipsum Loader's signature evasion: ships a 2017-era Node.js (v7.10.1) inside the ClickFix-delivered ZIP and uses it to execute the JavaScript payload, bypassing AV that whitelists modern signed node.exe. Hunts for any node.exe running from %TEMP%/%APPDATA%/Downloads with the legacy v7.x ProductVersion. Rationale: Article explicitly names "an outdated version of Node.js released in 2017 (version 7.10.1)" as the Lorem Ipsum Loader execution mechanism. Combination of node.exe + user-writable path is rare on corporate fleets — developers usually run from Program Files, AppData\Local\Programs\, or nvm directories with the current LTS.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1218 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running a portable Node.js extracted into a project folder under their user profile
  • Electron-based app (Slack, VS Code, Postman) running its embedded node helper from %APPDATA%
  • CI/CD agent or nvm-managed node interpreter under %APPDATA%\nvm\
  • npm install of native modules invoking node-gyp from project node_modules
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("slack.exe", "code.exe", "postman.exe", "discord.exe", "teams.exe") or FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Programs\", @"\nvm\", @"\node_modules\"))
Response runbook
Triage: Read ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion — anything starting with 7.x is the Lorem Ipsum tell. Diff the SHA256 against the official Node.js v7.10.1 win-x64 release hash; check what JavaScript file was passed on the cmdline and where it sits on disk. Contain: Isolate the host, kill node.exe + parent powershell.exe tree, quarantine the ZIP it was extracted from. Vanilla Tempest hands off to Rhysida ransomware — speed matters. Hunt: Pivot on the user across the prior 4h for the originating ClickFix Edge "security update" lure URL; check other hosts that hit the same compromised WordPress sites (architecture/legal/construction-tech sectors per BlueVoyant report).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend IsLegacyNode = (ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion startswith "7.10" or ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion startswith "7." or isempty(ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion))
| where IsLegacyNode
   or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Node.js Foundation"
   or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Node.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\AppData\\", "\\Temp\\", "\\Downloads\\", "\\Users\\Public\\", "\\ProgramData\\")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Outdated Node.js Executed From User-Writable Path
id: 8a4f1d2c-3b5e-49a7-9d6b-2e8f4a1c7d35
status: experimental
description: Lorem Ipsum Loader bundles an outdated 2017 Node.js (v7.10.1) inside its ClickFix-delivered ZIP to execute the JavaScript dropper payload, evading EDR that allowlists modern signed node.exe. Flags any node.exe running from %TEMP%, %APPDATA%, %DOWNLOADS%, %PROGRAMDATA%, or %PUBLIC%.

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\node\.exe$/i

DLL side-load of mscoree.dll or msvcp140.dll from non-System32 path (Lorem Ipsum) AIInstallation High
Lorem Ipsum Loader's batch-script persistence drops a malicious mscoree.dll or msvcp140.dll alongside a legitimate signed binary in a user-writable directory, then launches that binary so it loads the rogue DLL via search-order hijack. Detects image loads of these specific Windows runtime DLLs from anywhere other than the System32/SysWOW64/WinSxS/Program Files locations they legitimately live in. Rationale: Article explicitly names "mscoree.dll" and "msvcp140.dll" as the DLLs hijacked in the Lorem Ipsum side-load chain to decode the embedded loader. These two specific runtime DLLs are the highest-fidelity strings the article gives us — they should never legitimately load from %APPDATA%/%TEMP%/%PUBLIC%.
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable .NET app extracted to a user folder that ships a private mscoree shim (very rare in enterprise)
  • Indie game launcher bundling its own msvcp140.dll in a Public Documents games folder
  • Setup wizard temporarily extracting runtime DLLs to %TEMP% during MSI install
  • Legitimate vendor app installed under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\<vendor>\ shipping msvcp140 redistributable
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("setup.exe", "installer.exe", "msiexec.exe", "vc_redist.x64.exe", "vcredist_x86.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Microsoft\\EdgeUpdate\\"
Response runbook
Triage: Read the InitiatingProcess image — note the legit-looking signed binary it hijacks (often a small utility like 7zG.exe, Acrobat helpers, etc.). Hash both the host binary and the side-loaded DLL; submit DLL to sandbox to confirm Lorem Ipsum Loader payload (it should decode and reach out to a social-network profile URL). Contain: Isolate host, quarantine the entire folder containing both binaries, kill the host process. Check Run/RunOnce + Scheduled Tasks for the batch script that launches the side-load chain. Hunt: Look for the same SHA256 across the fleet (mass distribution), the originating ZIP in %DOWNLOADS%, and Edge browser history for the Edge "security update" lure URL that delivered it.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("mscoree.dll", "msvcp140.dll")
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("mscoree.dll", "msvcp140.dll")
| where TargetFilePath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32"
| where TargetFilePath !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64"
| where TargetFilePath !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS"
| where TargetFilePath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Side-Load of mscoree.dll or msvcp140.dll From User-Writable Path
id: 9b5e6f3a-7c2d-4e1b-8a9f-3d4c6b8e2a47
status: experimental
description: Lorem Ipsum Loader's persistence chain plants a malicious mscoree.dll or msvcp140.dll next to a legitimate signed application in a user-writable directory and triggers a search-order hijack to decode the embedded loader payload. These specific runtime DLLs should only ever load from System32/SysWOW64/WinSxS/Program Files.

falsepositives:
  - Standalone .NET application installed into a user profile that ships its own mscoree shim (rare)
  - Game launchers / portable apps that bundle a private msvcp140.dll
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:7 (@ImageLoaded:*\\mscoree.dll OR @ImageLoaded:*\\MSCOREE.DLL OR @ImageLoaded:*\\msvcp140.dll OR @ImageLoaded:*\\MSVCP140.DLL) (@ImageLoaded:*\\AppData\\* OR @ImageLoaded:*\\Temp\\* OR @ImageLoaded:*\\Downloads\\* OR @ImageLoaded:*\\Users\\Public\\* OR @ImageLoaded:*\\ProgramData\\*) -@ImageLoaded:C\:\\Windows\\System32\\* -@ImageLoaded:C\:\\Windows\\SysWOW64\\* -@ImageLoaded:C\:\\Program\ Files*
#event_simpleName=ImageHash OR #event_simpleName=ClassifiedModuleLoad
| TargetFileName=/\\(mscoree|msvcp140)\.dll$/i
| regex("\\\\(AppData|Temp|Downloads|Users\\\\Public|ProgramData)\\\\", field=TargetFileName)
| NOT regex("^C:\\\\Windows\\\\(System32|SysWOW64|WinSxS|Microsoft\\.NET)\\\\", field=TargetFileName)
| NOT regex("^C:\\\\Program Files", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT
`sysmon` EventCode=7 ImageLoaded IN ("*\\mscoree.dll", "*\\msvcp140.dll") NOT ImageLoaded IN ("C:\\Windows\\System32\\*", "C:\\Windows\\SysWOW64\\*", "C:\\Windows\\WinSxS\\*", "C:\\Program Files\\*", "C:\\Program Files (x86)\\*") (Image="*\\AppData\\*" OR Image="*\\Temp\\*" OR Image="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Image="*\\Users\\Public\\*" OR Image="*\\ProgramData\\*") | stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Image) as Image values(ImageLoaded) as ImageLoaded values(User) as User count by Computer | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Potemkin host-marker file %LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver creation AIInstallation High
Potemkin loader writes a per-victim UUID to %LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver as its host identifier for C2 polling. The filename masquerades as a Hyper-V configuration artifact but Hyper-V never writes anything under %LOCALAPPDATA% — making this a near-zero-FP marker for Potemkin installation. Rationale: Article directly names "%LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver" as the file Potemkin writes its UUID to for victim identification. Hyper-V config files live under %PROGRAMDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Hyper-V\ and the VM root paths — never %LOCALAPPDATA% — so this name+path combo is near-deterministic for Potemkin presence.
ATT&CKT1082 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • No legitimate scenario identified — flag every hit
  • Theoretical: a forensic analyst manually creating the file to reproduce IR scenarios
  • Theoretical: another malware family copy-catting Potemkin's marker filename
Response runbook
Triage: Note the InitiatingProcess — Potemkin's loader runs out of MSI/HTA → reflective load, so the writer is often rundll32.exe, regsvr32.exe, or a renamed binary in %APPDATA%. Read the file contents (it's the victim UUID, useful for cross-host correlation). Contain: Isolate immediately — Potemkin reflectively loads follow-on modules (RMMProject, EtherRAT) for credential theft. Kill all child processes of the writer. Hunt: Search %LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver across the entire fleet for the same UUID file — same UUID across hosts means re-imaging from a poisoned baseline. Pivot on the UUID string in DNS query patterns (Potemkin DGA uses a 1,000-word dictionary so look for clusters of ~10 dictionary-word lookups from the same host).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "hyper-v.ver"
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "hyper-v.ver"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\AppData\Local\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Potemkin Loader Host UUID Marker File
id: 4c8d9e7b-2a1f-4b6e-9d3c-5f7a8b1e3d49
status: experimental
description: Potemkin loader writes its per-victim UUID identifier to %LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver for DGA-driven C2 polling. The filename impersonates a Hyper-V configuration file but Hyper-V never writes to %LOCALAPPDATA%, making this a high-fidelity infection marker.
references:

author: SOC Detection Team

tags:

logsource:

  product: windows
detection:

    TargetFilename|endswith: '\hyper-v.ver'
    TargetFilename|contains: '\AppData\Local\'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:

level: critical
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:*\\hyper-v.ver OR @TargetFilename:*\\Hyper-V.ver OR @TargetFilename:*\\HYPER-V.VER) (@TargetFilename:*\\AppData\\Local\\* OR @TargetFilename:*\\appdata\\local\\*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\hyper-v\.ver$/i
| TargetFileName=/\\AppData\\Local\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime FROM datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem WHERE Filesystem.action=created AND Filesystem.file_name=hyper-v.ver AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\AppData\\Local\\*" BY Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
MSI installer spawning HTA payload (Potemkin delivery chain) AIExploitation High
Potemkin's delivery sequence: ClickFix lures the user into running an MSI, msiexec.exe extracts and executes an HTA payload via mshta.exe, and the HTA reflectively loads the Potemkin x64 loader. msiexec spawning mshta is virtually unheard of in legitimate software installs. Rationale: Article describes Potemkin attack chain as "installs an MSI package, which then drops a previously undocumented loader codenamed Potemkin via an HTML Application (HTA) payload." The msiexec → mshta parent-child relationship is the cleanest article-derived behavioural anchor.
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1218.005 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy enterprise MSI that bundles an HTA-based install UI (very rare; mostly pre-2010 packages)
  • Custom in-house deployment package that uses an HTA dialog as part of post-install configuration
  • Vendor MSI that runs a license-prompt HTA via mshta as a custom action
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("corp.local", "\\\\fileserver\\", "sccm", "intune")
Response runbook
Triage: Capture the HTA URL/path from mshta.exe cmdline and the originating MSI path from msiexec cmdline. Sandbox the MSI to confirm Potemkin behaviour (DGA C2, hyper-v.ver write). Check Edge/Chrome download history to identify the ClickFix lure that delivered the MSI. Contain: Isolate the host, kill the msiexec/mshta tree, quarantine both MSI and any dropped binaries. Hunt: Look for %LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver creation, EtherRAT or Lua-scripted RMMProject artifacts, and DGA-style DNS bursts (many dictionary-word lookups in short time window) on this and adjacent hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where FileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\msiexec.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: HTA Payload Spawned by MSI Installer (Potemkin Loader Chain)
id: 6e3a8c4d-1f7b-4d2e-9a5c-7b8e4f1d9c52
status: experimental
description: Potemkin loader is delivered through an MSI package that drops and executes an HTA payload via mshta.exe — the HTA then reflectively loads the x64 loader stage. msiexec.exe spawning mshta.exe is virtually nonexistent in legitimate software installs.
references:

author: SOC Detection Team
date: 2026/06/17
tags:

  - attack.t1218.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\msiexec.exe'
    Image|endswith: '\mshta.exe'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Custom enterprise MSI packages that invoke HTA-based UI dialogs during install (extremely rare)
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\msiexec.exe OR *\\MsiExec.exe OR *\\MSIEXEC.EXE) @Image:(*\\mshta.exe OR *\\MSHTA.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/msiexec\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/\\mshta\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, ParentImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime FROM datamodel=Endpoint.Processes WHERE Processes.parent_process_name=msiexec.exe AND Processes.process_name=mshta.exe BY Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime FROM datamodel=Endpoint.Processes WHERE Processes.parent_process_name=msiexec.exe AND Processes.process_name=mshta.exe BY Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Storage Crypter external-storage payload read (BabaDeda List.Control.dat) AIInstallation Medium
BabaDeda's second-stage 'Storage Crypter' component reads its encrypted payload from external storage-like files (e.g. List.Control.dat) co-located with a legitimate-looking signed binary, decoding only moments before execution to minimise forensic visibility. Hunts for any process reading a *.Control.dat file outside well-known software-install paths. Rationale: Article directly names "List.Control.dat" as the external storage file BabaDeda's Storage Crypter reads to retrieve the encoded payload — Morphisec quote: "reads the payload material from external storage-like files such as 'List.Control.dat'." Specific filename pattern is the lowest-FP behavioural anchor for this novel loader-decomposition pattern.
ATT&CKT1140 T1027.009
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom enterprise software using .Control.dat as a config/data file naming convention (uncommon)
  • Forensic researcher or sandbox analyst manually placing/inspecting the file for reproduction
  • Legacy CAD/CAM or industrial-control software using .Control.dat for instrument lists
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe", "searchindexer.exe", "backup.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
Response runbook
Triage: Read the InitiatingProcess image — Storage Crypter pairs the .dat with a benign-looking signed binary in the same folder. Hash both. Read first 512 bytes of the .dat: high-entropy non-printable data with no clear file magic = encoded payload. Contain: Isolate host, quarantine entire folder (binary + .dat), kill InitiatingProcess tree. BabaDeda has historically led to LockBit and infostealers (target sectors: education, finance per April 2026 Morphisec report). Hunt: Search the fleet for the same SHA256 of the host binary and the .dat hash; check svchost.exe child processes on the host (BabaDeda injects into svchost.exe); pivot on the user for ClickFix PowerShell entry within the prior 24h.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "List.Control.dat" or FileName endswith ".Control.dat"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" or isempty(InitiatingProcessAccountName)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "List.Control.dat" or TargetFileName endswith ".Control.dat"
| where TargetFilePath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
| where TargetFilePath !startswith @"C:\Windows"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: BabaDeda Storage Crypter External Payload File Access
id: 5d2e9f1c-8b3a-4c7e-a6d8-9e1f3b5c7a64
status: experimental
description: BabaDeda's Storage Crypter stage reads its encrypted payload material from external storage-like .Control.dat files (e.g. List.Control.dat) co-located with a benign-looking signed binary, decoding only moments before execution. Hunts file accesses to *.Control.dat outside legitimate software-install paths.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/clickfix-campaigns-expand-malware.html
author: SOC Detection Team
date: 2026/06/17
tags:

logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_name:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\List.Control.dat'
      - '.Control.dat'
  filter_legit:
    TargetFilename|startswith:
      - 'C:\Program Files\'
      - 'C:\Program Files (x86)\'
      - 'C:\Windows\'
  condition: selection_name and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
  - Niche legitimate software using .Control.dat naming convention in user-writable paths (none commonly observed)
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:(11 OR 15) (@TargetFilename:*\\List.Control.dat OR @TargetFilename:*.Control.dat) -@TargetFilename:C\:\\Program\ Files* -@TargetFilename:C\:\\Windows\\*
(#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo OR #event_simpleName=FileWritten)
| TargetFileName=/\\(List\.)?Control\.dat$/i
| NOT TargetFileName=/^C:\\Program Files/i
| NOT TargetFileName=/^C:\\Windows\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime FROM datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem WHERE (Filesystem.file_name="List.Control.dat" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.Control.dat") BY Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.action Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search file_path!="*\\Program Files\\*" file_path!="*\\Windows\\*" | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime FROM datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem WHERE (Filesystem.file_name="List.Control.dat" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.Control.dat") BY Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.action Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search file_path!="*\\Program Files\\*" file_path!="*\\Windows\\*" | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("95.163.152.190", "91.92.243.161") or RemoteUrl has_any ("malicious.site")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["95.163.152.190", "91.92.243.161"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["malicious.site"]);
ImNetworkSession

| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)

| order by TimeGenerated desc

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

vLLM CVE-2026-48746 auth bypass via malformed Host header on /v1/* (`/` or `?` in Host) AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact exploitation primitive in CVE-2026-48746: HTTP requests to a vLLM OpenAI-compatible endpoint where the Host header carries reserved URL characters (`/`, `?`) that the attacker injects to make starlette's `URL(scope=scope).path` resolve to a non-`/v1` path while FastAPI routing still serves the `/v1` API. Targets vLLM 0.3.0 ≤ v < 0.22.0 directly exposed (no RFC-conforming reverse proxy in front). Rationale: Article body explicitly names the bypass primitive: 'an attacker to include special URL characters such as `/` or `?` in the Host: header'. Any inbound request to `/v1/*` with `/` or `?` in the Host header is RFC-7230-non-compliant and points directly at CVE-2026-48746 exploitation; the GHSA advisory itself is the authoritative second source for the affected range (vllm 0.3.0 ≤ v < 0.22.0). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94f4-hr76-p5j6
ATT&CKT1190 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Misconfigured upstream proxy that forwards a virtual-host string containing a path segment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Nessus, Tenable, Qualys) running the CVE-2026-48746 plugin
  • Pen-test / red-team reproducing the PoC during an authorised engagement
  • Old IIS server bug where Host header is set to URL fragment by a legacy client (rare)
  • Custom internal tooling that uses host:port/path style proxying
Suppression filter
// suppress known scanners and internal pen-test source ranges
| where SrcIp !in ("<vuln_scanner_ip>", "<redteam_jumphost_ip>")
| where HostHdr !startswith "qualys" and HostHdr !startswith "nessus"
Response runbook
1. Triage: pivot on SrcIp — pull all /v1/* requests from that source in the last 24h, decode the Host header to see the injected path/query, check whether HTTP 200 responses followed (successful bypass) vs 4xx (blocked). 2. Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge, take the vLLM instance off the internet (revoke NSG/SG public ingress) until you can place an RFC-conforming proxy (nginx, ALB) in front per the advisory's mitigation note. 3. Hunt: enumerate every vLLM deployment via DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory where SoftwareName=='vllm' and SoftwareVersion < 0.22.0, audit which are internet-facing without a reverse proxy, review their access logs for the same Host-header pattern across the last 30 days, and check the model/prompt logs for unexpected inference calls that may indicate model-theft or data-exfil during the bypass window.
// vLLM CVE-2026-48746 — Host header carrying / or ? against a vLLM /v1/* endpoint
// Path 1: nginx/vllm access logs shipped via Syslog
let vllm_syslog =
    Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where SyslogMessage has "/v1/"
    | extend HostHdr = extract(@'"Host:\s*([^"\r\n]+)"', 1, SyslogMessage)
    | extend ReqPath = extract(@'"(?:GET|POST|PUT|DELETE)\s+(/v1/[^\s"]+)', 1, SyslogMessage)
    | extend SrcIp   = extract(@'(\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)', 1, SyslogMessage)
    | where isnotempty(ReqPath)
    | where HostHdr matches regex @"[/?]"      // RFC 7230 forbids these in Host header
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SrcIp, HostHdr, ReqPath, SyslogMessage;
// Path 2: CEF/WAF in front of vLLM
let vllm_cef =
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL has "/v1/"
    | where DestinationHostName matches regex @"[/?]"
    | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, DeviceProduct;
union vllm_syslog, vllm_cef
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: vLLM Auth Bypass via Malformed Host Header (CVE-2026-48746)
id: 7d3a8c41-9f06-4a2b-b8a4-2e7d6f1a9c10
status: experimental
description: Detects HTTP requests against vLLM /v1/* endpoints where the Host header contains reserved URL characters ('/' or '?') used to bypass starlette AuthenticationMiddleware (CVE-2026-48746).

  - Misconfigured reverse proxy passing through SNI-style virtual host values
  - Internal pen testers validating the CVE

vLLM /v1/* API access without Authorization header on auth-configured instance AIExploitation Medium
Hunts requests to vLLM OpenAI-compatible API endpoints (/v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions, /v1/models, /v1/embeddings) that arrive without an Authorization: Bearer header on a deployment that has VLLM_API_KEY / --api-key set. Successful 200 responses under these conditions are a direct symptom of CVE-2026-48746 exploitation or other middleware misconfiguration. Rationale: Article states the bypass 'allows to use the API without providing the configured VLLM_API_KEY or --api-key'. Endpoint set is the documented OpenAI-compatible surface vLLM exposes under /v1. A 200 with no Authorization Bearer on these paths is the post-bypass signature; correlates the reviewer-suggested credential-access pivot to the article's specific endpoints. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94f4-hr76-p5j6 • https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/serving/openai_compatible_server.html
ATT&CKT1556 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • vLLM deployments intentionally running without API key (legitimate, no auth configured)
  • Health-check probes from Kubernetes liveness/readiness hitting /v1/models without auth
  • Internal monitoring tooling using IP allowlist instead of bearer auth
  • Load balancer health pings
  • Initial /v1/models discovery calls from approved client SDKs before they read the token from env
Suppression filter
| where SrcIp !in ("<k8s_node_cidr>", "<healthcheck_lb_ip>")
| where SyslogMessage !contains "kube-probe"
| where SyslogMessage !contains "ELB-HealthChecker"
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the target vLLM instance has VLLM_API_KEY or --api-key set (check systemd unit, docker-compose, or k8s manifest env) — if no API key is configured, this is by design, suppress and tag the host. 2. Contain: if API key IS configured, treat as confirmed bypass — block the source IP at edge, rotate VLLM_API_KEY, restart vLLM, and front the listener with nginx per advisory mitigation. 3. Hunt: pull all /v1/chat/completions and /v1/completions bodies from the suspect window — look for prompts that exfiltrate system prompts, leak training data via membership inference, or attempt prompt injection chains. Check egress for the same source pulling /v1/models repeatedly (recon).
// vLLM /v1/* requests lacking Authorization: Bearer that succeeded (200)
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/v1/chat/completions","/v1/completions","/v1/models","/v1/embeddings")
| extend ReqMethod = extract(@'"(GET|POST|PUT|DELETE)\s', 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend ReqPath   = extract(@'"(?:GET|POST|PUT|DELETE)\s+(/v1/[^\s"]+)', 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend Status    = toint(extract(@'"\s(\d{3})\s', 1, SyslogMessage))
| extend SrcIp     = extract(@'^(\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)', 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend HasAuth   = SyslogMessage matches regex @'(?i)authorization:\s*Bearer\s+\S+'
| where isnotempty(ReqPath)
| where Status == 200
| where HasAuth == false
| summarize Requests=count(), Paths=make_set(ReqPath, 10), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIp, Computer
| where Requests >= 1
| order by Requests desc
title: vLLM /v1 API Request Without Authorization Header
id: 9b1f0d52-3e08-46c5-9d18-7c2a5b6e88f1
status: experimental
description: Detects HTTP requests against vLLM OpenAI-compatible /v1/* endpoints that lack an Authorization Bearer token, indicative of CVE-2026-48746 bypass when the deployment has VLLM_API_KEY configured.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:

logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:

      - '/v1/completions'

  - Health check probes hitting /v1/models with no auth (filter by user-agent)
level: medium
source:(nginx OR vllm OR haproxy) @http.url_details.path:(\/v1\/chat\/completions OR \/v1\/completions OR \/v1\/models OR \/v1\/embeddings) @http.status_code:200 -@http.headers.authorization:Bearer\ *
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents values(Web.status) as status_codes from datamodel=Web where Web.url IN ("*/v1/chat/completions","*/v1/completions","*/v1/models","*/v1/embeddings","*/v1/audio/*") by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | join type=outer src [ search index=proxy sourcetype=nginx_access uri_path IN ("/v1/chat/completions","/v1/completions","/v1/models") NOT "authorization" | stats values(src) as src by src ] | where mvfind(status_codes, "200")>=0 AND mvfind(status_codes, "401")<0 | eval reason="vLLM /v1/* served 200 with no Authorization header observed"

vLLM 401/403 followed by 200 on /v1/* from same source IP within short window AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the exploitation timeline of CVE-2026-48746: an attacker first probes vLLM auth (receiving 401/403 because they have no token), then within a short window obtains 200 responses on the same /v1/* endpoints from the same source IP without ever presenting valid credentials. Encodes the failure→success transition the reviewer flagged. Rationale: Reviewer suggestion 3, anchored to the article's auth-bypass narrative. A single source IP receiving 401/403 then 200 on /v1/* within 10 minutes — without a credential change — is exactly the exploit timeline the article describes (probe → bypass via Host header → unauthorised inference). Time-window correlation cuts the broad 'no Authorization header' baseline noise. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94f4-hr76-p5j6
ATT&CKT1556 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User mistyped API key, fixed it, and continued (legitimate fix)
  • Client SDK rotating to a freshly-issued token mid-session
  • Health probe failing then a real authenticated client succeeding shortly after (NAT/proxy sharing source IP)
  • Intermittent reverse-proxy auth header stripping on retry
  • CI pipeline fetching a token from a vault between failure and retry
Suppression filter
| where SrcIp !in ("<corp_nat_gateway>", "<ci_runner_egress_ip>")
| extend FailHasToken = SyslogMessage matches regex @'(?i)authorization:\s*Bearer\s+\S+'
| where FailHasToken == false  // only the credential-less failure->success path
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the raw request lines for both the failing and succeeding calls from this SrcIp — compare the Authorization header values. If the failures had NO Authorization and the successes also had NO Authorization (or the same invalid one), this is the bypass; if the failures had an invalid token and successes had a valid one, it's a benign credential fix. 2. Contain: on confirmed bypass, block SrcIp at edge, rotate VLLM_API_KEY, and deploy nginx in front per advisory mitigation. 3. Hunt: enumerate every /v1/chat/completions body from SrcIp in the success window, look for prompts probing internal data or system-prompt extraction; check whether SrcIp also performed Host-header injection (correlate to UC1) — co-occurrence is high-confidence exploitation evidence.
// Auth failure -> success transition on vLLM /v1/* from the same source IP within 10 min
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
let vllm_reqs =
    Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where SyslogMessage has "/v1/"
    | extend ReqPath = extract(@'"(?:GET|POST|PUT|DELETE)\s+(/v1/[^\s"]+)', 1, SyslogMessage)
    | extend Status  = toint(extract(@'"\s(\d{3})\s', 1, SyslogMessage))
    | extend SrcIp   = extract(@'^(\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)', 1, SyslogMessage)
    | where isnotempty(ReqPath) and isnotempty(SrcIp);
let failures =
    vllm_reqs
    | where Status in (401, 403)
    | project FailTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIp, Computer, FailPath = ReqPath;
let successes =
    vllm_reqs
    | where Status in (200, 201)
    | project SuccTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIp, Computer, SuccPath = ReqPath;
failures
| join kind=inner successes on SrcIp, Computer
| where SuccTime between (FailTime .. FailTime + WindowMinutes)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', SuccTime, FailTime)
| summarize FailCount=count(), FirstFail=min(FailTime), FirstSuccess=min(SuccTime), Paths=make_set(SuccPath, 10) by SrcIp, Computer
| where FailCount >= 1
| order by FirstSuccess desc

Langflow CVE-2026-48519: POST to /api/v1/build_public_tmp with embedded Python code AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated exploitation of Langflow's Shareable Playground RCE. The exploit POSTs to /api/v1/build_public_tmp/<flow-id>/flow with a JSON body whose data.nodes[].data.node.template.code.value field carries arbitrary Python — fires on the exact endpoint+payload pattern named in the advisory PoC. Rationale: Hardcoded to the literal endpoint path '/api/v1/build_public_tmp' named in the GHSA advisory body and PoC cURL. POST/PUT-only because the vulnerable code path requires a JSON body with the malicious nodes[].data.node.template.code.value field. Cross-checked with NVD entry for CVE-2026-48519 and the langflow-ai/langflow GitHub release notes for 1.9.1. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v5ff-9q35-q26f • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48519 • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user accessing a Shareable Playground link they were intentionally given
  • Langflow developer testing flows locally during development
  • Internal QA/load-testing tools exercising the endpoint
  • Browser auto-replays of saved POST requests from devtools session
  • Vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys) probing the path for CVE-2026-48519
Suppression filter
| where not (ClientIP in ("<known-admin-ip-1>","<known-admin-ip-2>") and UserAgent has_any ("Mozilla","Chrome","Firefox") and BytesIn < 2048)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full POST body for the matching request and check whether data.nodes[].data.node.template.code.value contains Python builtins (exec, eval, __import__, subprocess, os.system, socket) or shell tokens (touch, curl, wget, bash, /tmp/, /dev/shm). A benign Shareable Playground click sends only stock chat-input wiring. Step 2 (contain): If malicious payload confirmed, block the source IP at the edge, disable the affected public flow (DELETE on the flow's public_id), and isolate the Langflow host pending forensics. If patch is available, upgrade to >1.9.1 immediately. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the Langflow host's outbound network for the next 24h for any new domains/IPs, check /tmp /dev/shm and the Langflow working directory for new files, and grep langflow logs for other public flow IDs hit by the same client_id cookie or source IP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp" or AdditionalFields has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let LangflowHits_IIS = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where csUriStem has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp"
    | where csMethod in~ ("POST","PUT")
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = Computer, ClientIP = cIP, UriStem = csUriStem, UriQuery = csUriQuery, Method = csMethod, Status = scStatus, UserAgent = csUserAgent, BytesIn = csBytes;
let LangflowHits_CEF = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp"
    | where RequestMethod in~ ("POST","PUT")
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = DestinationHostName, ClientIP = SourceIP, UriStem = RequestURL, UriQuery = RequestContext, Method = RequestMethod, Status = tostring(EventOutcome), UserAgent = RequestClientApplication, BytesIn = ReceivedBytes;
union isfuzzy=true LangflowHits_IIS, LangflowHits_CEF
| extend SuspiciousPayloadSize = iff(BytesIn > 1024, true, false)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow exploit reconnaissance: clustered errors against /api/v1/build_public_tmp AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects burst of HTTP 4xx/5xx responses from the Langflow /api/v1/build_public_tmp endpoint by a single source IP — the failure signature of attackers iterating flow IDs or malformed JSON payloads before landing a working CVE-2026-48519 exploit. Tunable threshold; defaults to >=10 errors per source IP within 10 minutes. Rationale: Pre-RCE recon shape — attackers iterating flow IDs (404), JSON shape (400), or malformed payloads (500) against the literal endpoint path '/api/v1/build_public_tmp' the advisory names. Threshold of 10/10min separates scanner activity from a single user re-clicking a stale share link. Cross-checked NVD CVE-2026-48519 detail and the langflow repository's build_public_tmp route handler. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v5ff-9q35-q26f • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48519
ATT&CKT1190 T1595.002
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner sweep (Tenable/Qualys/Rapid7) probing for CVE-2026-48519
  • User repeatedly clicking a Shareable Playground link after the underlying flow was deleted (404 loop)
  • Frontend SPA bug causing a request retry loop against the endpoint
  • WAF blocking legitimate requests and generating 403s in a burst
  • Health-check / monitoring tools probing the endpoint without a valid flow ID
Suppression filter
| where ClientIP !in ("<scanner-ip-1>","<scanner-ip-2>") and UserAgent !has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Nuclei","masscan","healthcheck")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Look up the source IP in threat intel (Shodan, AbuseIPDB, internal IOC list) and check what HTTP status codes dominate the burst — pure 404s suggest flow-ID guessing, mixed 400/500 suggests payload fuzzing, pure 403 suggests WAF blocking. Step 2 (contain): If external + non-scanner, block the source IP at the WAF/edge and rate-limit the /api/v1/build_public_tmp path globally. If internal, identify the scanner and exclude the IP from this rule. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the source IP for any successful (HTTP 200) calls to the same endpoint in the surrounding 30 minutes — those are the exploitation attempt that landed. Cross-reference with UC1 (POST to /api/v1/build_public_tmp).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp"
| summarize HitCount = count(), Hosts = make_set(DeviceName, 10), Procs = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 5)
          by RemoteIP, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where HitCount >= 10
| order by Timestamp desc
let WindowSize = 10m;
let Threshold = 10;
let IIS_Errors = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where csUriStem has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp"
    | where scStatus >= 400
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = Computer, ClientIP = cIP, UriStem = csUriStem, Status = tostring(scStatus), UserAgent = csUserAgent;
let CEF_Errors = CommonSecurityLog

    | where RequestURL has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp"
    | where toint(coalesce(DeviceCustomString1, "0")) >= 400 or EventOutcome in ("4","5","Failure")
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = DestinationHostName, ClientIP = SourceIP, UriStem = RequestURL, Status = tostring(EventOutcome), UserAgent = RequestClientApplication;
union isfuzzy=true IIS_Errors, CEF_Errors
| summarize ErrorCount = count(), StatusCodes = make_set(Status, 20), UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 10), Hosts = make_set(Host, 5), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by ClientIP, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowSize)
| where ErrorCount >= Threshold
| order by LastSeen desc
