Wallpaper Engine spawning script interpreters or LOLBins from workshop content AIExploitation Medium
Broader hunting query for the 'application wallpaper' execution model described in the article — Wallpaper Engine launches user-supplied executables that may chain to cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe, rundll32.exe, or other interpreters. Application wallpapers from Steam Workshop should never legitimately need a script interpreter; this hunts the entire campaign pattern beyond the specific Synaptics/cache_GAME1 filenames. Rationale: Article: 'Application wallpapers are essentially standalone programs' and 'allows foreign code to be run directly on your computer'. Wallpaper Engine itself has no legitimate need to spawn cmd/powershell/wscript — these parent-child pairs are a clean campaign indicator. Catches variants that don't reuse the Synaptics/_cache_GAME1 names from UC1.
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Wallpaper Engine 'Workshop' page launch invoking rundll32.exe for Windows shell preview thumbnails (rare but possible on first-time workshop browsing)
  • Legitimate scene wallpaper using a small PowerShell helper to query system stats (e.g., custom CPU/GPU monitor widget) — should be allow-listed by SHA256 of the workshop entry
  • Wallpaper Engine config repair launching cmd.exe to flush a corrupted cache
  • Steam Big Picture mode launching wallpaper through a shell wrapper
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--update-check","--repair-cache","thumbnail"))
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Pull the full command line — if it contains base64-encoded PowerShell, references a URL, or drops anything to %TEMP%/%APPDATA%, treat as confirmed. Hash the parent .exe (the workshop application wallpaper) and check against the IOC bundle. 2. CONTAIN: Suspend wallpaper32/64.exe, kill child processes, isolate host, snapshot \Steam\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\ subscription directories for forensic analysis. 3. HUNT: Identify the workshop subscription ID and check whether other users in the org downloaded the same wallpaper — pivot on the workshop folder GUID across DeviceFileEvents.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe","webwallpaper32.exe","webwallpaper64.exe","wallpaperservice32_c.exe","wallpaperservice64_c.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
   or (FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\Users\Public\") and FileName endswith ".exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(web)?wallpaper(32|64)(_c)?\.exe$" or ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\wallpaperservice(32|64)_c\.exe$"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32|bitsadmin|certutil|curl|wget)\.exe$"
   or ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(AppData\\Local\\Temp|AppData\\Roaming|Users\\Public)\\[^\\]+\.exe$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Wallpaper Engine Spawning Script Interpreter or LOLBin
id: 2f8d4e3a-6b1c-4a9f-92c5-8e3d1f7b6a44
status: experimental
description: Wallpaper Engine application/scene wallpaper executes a Windows script interpreter or LOLBin. Application wallpapers from Steam Workshop should never legitimately require these binaries.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/dozens-of-malicious-wallpapers-found-on-steam-workshop/120186/
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1059.003
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\wallpaper32.exe'
      - '\wallpaper64.exe'
      - '\webwallpaper32.exe'
      - '\webwallpaper64.exe'
      - '\wallpaperservice32_c.exe'
      - '\wallpaperservice64_c.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\rundll32.exe'
      - '\regsvr32.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\wget.exe'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\wallpaper32.exe OR *\wallpaper64.exe OR *\webwallpaper32.exe OR *\webwallpaper64.exe OR *\Wallpaper32.exe OR *\Wallpaper64.exe) @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\wscript.exe OR *\cscript.exe OR *\mshta.exe OR *\rundll32.exe OR *\regsvr32.exe OR *\bitsadmin.exe OR *\certutil.exe OR *\curl.exe OR *\wget.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\CMD.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/(web)?wallpaper(32|64)(_c)?\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32|bitsadmin|certutil|curl|wget)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe","webwallpaper32.exe","webwallpaper64.exe") AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe") by host Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe","webwallpaper32.exe","webwallpaper64.exe") AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe") by host Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Persistence via Run key referencing Wallpaper Engine / Synaptics / NTRaholic paths AIInstallation Medium
Detects autostart registry writes (Run / RunOnce / Image File Execution Options) that reference the artifacts named in the Kaspersky article — Synaptics.exe outside the legit Synaptics folder, ._cache_GAME1.exe, or any value pointing into \steamapps\workshop\content\431960\ (Wallpaper Engine's workshop directory). DarkKomet's classic Run-key persistence anchored to this campaign's specific filenames. Rationale: Article: 'leave the victim's system infected with backdoors or crypto miners' — backdoors persist. DarkKomet's documented behavior is Run-key persistence, and the article names Synaptics.exe and ._cache_GAME1.exe as the dropped artifacts. Filtering out the legitimate Synaptics touchpad driver path keeps FP rate low.
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Synaptics touchpad driver Run key (HKCU\...\Run\SynTPEnh) — excluded by the \Program Files\Synaptics\ path filter
  • Steam itself registering a Run key referencing steamapps directory for game updaters
  • Wallpaper Engine adding its own Run key during install (under \Wallpaper Engine\wallpaper32.exe, NOT under \workshop\content\)
  • User manually adding NTRaholic to startup after legitimately installing the game from another source
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("steam.exe","steamservice.exe") or RegistryValueData !has @"\steamapps\common\"
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Inspect the InitiatingProcessFileName that wrote the registry value — if it's wallpaper32/64.exe, Synaptics.exe (outside the legit Synaptics directory), or ._cache_GAME1.exe, treat as confirmed. Capture the value data path and verify the binary exists. 2. CONTAIN: Delete the registry value, quarantine the file at the referenced path, kill any running instances, and isolate the host. Rotate the user's Steam password and revoke active sessions. 3. HUNT: Pivot the file SHA256 across DeviceProcessEvents to find first execution, check DeviceNetworkEvents for 120.48.156.17/202.144.192.29 callbacks, and hash-match all 13 IOCs across the fleet to find other infected endpoints.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\CurrentVersion\RunOnce", @"\Image File Execution Options\", @"\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\Shell", @"\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\Userinit")
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("Synaptics.exe","_cache_GAME1.exe","NTRaholic",@"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\")
| where not (RegistryValueData has @"\Program Files\Synaptics\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\CurrentVersion\RunOnce", @"\Image File Execution Options\", @"\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\Shell", @"\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\Userinit")
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("Synaptics.exe","_cache_GAME1.exe","NTRaholic",@"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\")
| where not (RegistryValueData has @"\Program Files\Synaptics\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Run Key Persistence Referencing Steam Workshop Wallpaper Malware Artifacts
id: 6a3f9c1d-4e8b-4d7f-b0a2-9c1d2e5f8b77
status: experimental
description: Autostart registry value written that references Synaptics.exe (outside legit Synaptics path), ._cache_GAME1.exe, NTRaholic, or the Wallpaper Engine workshop content directory.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/dozens-of-malicious-wallpapers-found-on-steam-workshop/120186/
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
  - attack.t1547.001
logsource:
  category: registry_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_key:
    TargetObject|contains:
      - '\CurrentVersion\Run\'
      - '\CurrentVersion\RunOnce\'
      - '\Image File Execution Options\'
      - '\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\Shell'
      - '\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\Userinit'
  selection_data:
    Details|contains:
      - 'Synaptics.exe'
      - '_cache_GAME1.exe'
      - 'NTRaholic'
      - '\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\'
  filter_legit_synaptics:
    Details|contains: '\Program Files\Synaptics\'
  condition: selection_key and selection_data and not filter_legit_synaptics
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:13 @TargetObject:(*\CurrentVersion\Run\* OR *\CurrentVersion\RunOnce\* OR *\Image File Execution Options\* OR *\currentversion\run\* OR *\currentversion\runonce\*) @Details:(*Synaptics.exe* OR *synaptics.exe* OR *_cache_GAME1.exe* OR *_cache_game1.exe* OR *NTRaholic* OR *ntraholic* OR *\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\*) -@Details:(*\Program Files\Synaptics\* OR *\program files\synaptics\*)
#event_simpleName=AsepValueUpdate
| RegObjectName=/\\CurrentVersion\\(Run|RunOnce)\\|\\Image File Execution Options\\|\\Winlogon\\(Shell|Userinit)/i
| RegStringValue=/Synaptics\.exe|_cache_GAME1\.exe|NTRaholic|\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\/i
| NOT RegStringValue=/\\Program Files\\Synaptics\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RegObjectName, RegValueName, RegStringValue, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path IN ("*\\CurrentVersion\\Run\\*","*\\CurrentVersion\\RunOnce\\*","*\\CurrentVersion\\Image File Execution Options\\*") AND (Registry.registry_value_data="*Synaptics.exe*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*_cache_GAME1.exe*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*NTRaholic*") by host Registry.user Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.registry_value_data Registry.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path IN ("*\\CurrentVersion\\Run\\*","*\\CurrentVersion\\RunOnce\\*","*\\CurrentVersion\\Image File Execution Options\\*") AND (Registry.registry_value_data="*Synaptics.exe*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*_cache_GAME1.exe*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*NTRaholic*") by host Registry.user Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.registry_value_data Registry.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("202.144.192.29", "120.48.156.17") or RemoteUrl has_any ("brightly.to")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["202.144.192.29", "120.48.156.17"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["brightly.to"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] WIN_DRV kernel driver service installed from non-system path · [LLM] SprySOCKS WIN_DRV / WIN_PLUS binary hash hit on Windows endpoint · [LLM] Boot Manager / BCD tampering indicative of CVE-2023-24932 BlackLotus-style UEFI bootkit · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] SprySOCKS Windows C2 egress to FishMonger infrastructure 207.148.78.36 / 207.148.75.122 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
SprySOCKS Windows C2 egress to FishMonger infrastructure 207.148.78.36 / 207.148.75.122 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound TCP/UDP connections from Windows endpoints to the hardcoded C&C IPs used by SprySOCKS WIN_DRV/WIN_PLUS variants. Article-specific because these are operator-controlled Vultr IPs baked into the backdoor's compiled configuration, not crawled telemetry. Rationale: Direct match on the two hardcoded C2 IPs (207.148.78.36 / 207.148.75.122) ESET published. These are operator-controlled Vultr addresses baked into the WIN_DRV/WIN_PLUS samples — no legitimate enterprise traffic should reach them. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1033/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/23/i/earth-lusca-employs-new-linux-backdoor.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1095
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / threat-intel team intentionally connecting to the IPs from a sandbox VM
  • Outbound NAT IP collisions if a corporate proxy briefly shared a /24 with Vultr
  • Vulnerability scanners targeting the IPs from a known-scanner host
  • Network device sending NetFlow/syslog through a Vultr-hosted aggregator
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("207.148.78.36","207.148.75.122")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull DeviceNetworkEvents around the hit and identify the InitiatingProcessFileName + folder path; check whether the binary is signed and whether parent is a service host or anomalous LOLBin. 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender MDE Machine Isolation, block both C2 IPs at the perimeter, capture memory and the binary for hash submission. 3) Hunt: pivot on the binary SHA256 across DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceFileEvents for the last 90 days; query DeviceRegistryEvents for new Services keys created by the same process; review DeviceLogonEvents for the user account around the C2 callback.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("207.148.78.36", "207.148.75.122")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let cc_ips = dynamic(["207.148.78.36", "207.148.75.122"]);
(union isfuzzy=true
    (CommonSecurityLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where DestinationIP in (cc_ips)
        | project TimeGenerated, SrcHost = SourceHostName, SrcIP = SourceIP, DstIP = DestinationIP, DstPort = DestinationPort, Proto = Protocol, App = DeviceProduct),
    (ImNetworkSession
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where DstIpAddr in (cc_ips)
        | project TimeGenerated, SrcHost = SrcHostname, SrcIP = SrcIpAddr, DstIP = DstIpAddr, DstPort = DstPortNumber, Proto = NetworkProtocol, App = EventProduct)
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WIN_DRV kernel driver service installed from non-system path AIInstallation High
SprySOCKS WIN_DRV loads a kernel driver to hide processes, files, registry keys and network connections. Detects service installation events (EID 7045 / 4697) where service type indicates a kernel-mode driver and the image path is outside the canonical Windows driver directories — the article calls out kernel-driver-based rootkit behaviour as the WIN_DRV signature. Rationale: Article specifies WIN_DRV uses kernel drivers to hide network connections, processes, files and registry keys. ServiceType=kernel + non-system path is the install signature. Excluding the four legitimate driver paths keeps FPs to genuinely rare WHQL-bypass or rootkit installs. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/003/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1014/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1014 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • VPN client installers (Cisco AnyConnect, GlobalProtect) dropping drivers under Program Files
  • Endpoint security tools (CrowdStrike, SentinelOne) installing kernel sensors
  • Virtualisation tooling (VMware Tools, VirtualBox guest additions) installing drivers from vendor folders
  • Hardware vendor drivers (Dell, HP) installed via OEM updater into Program Files\<Vendor>
Suppression filter
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$" | where ServiceFileName !has_any ("\\Program Files\\Cisco\\", "\\Program Files\\CrowdStrike\\", "\\Program Files\\VMware\\", "\\Program Files\\SentinelOne\\", "\\Program Files\\Palo Alto Networks\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the .sys file, verify Authenticode signer and WHQL status; pull EID 6 (Sysmon driver load) on the same host to confirm load succeeded. 2) Contain: if signer is untrusted or unsigned, isolate the host and submit the driver hash to threat intel; disable the service via Defender Live Response (sc.exe stop / delete). 3) Hunt: search DeviceNetworkEvents from the host for callbacks to 207.148.78.36 / 207.148.75.122; query DeviceFileEvents for the .sys hash across the fleet; check DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities for CVE-2023-24932 exposure on the same hosts.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("DriverLoad", "ServiceInstalled")
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32\drivers\"
    and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64\drivers\"
    and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32\DriverStore\"
| where FileName endswith ".sys"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4697
| where ServiceType has "kernel"
| where ServiceFileName !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32\drivers\"
    and ServiceFileName !startswith @"\??\C:\Windows\System32\drivers\"
    and ServiceFileName !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64\drivers\"
    and ServiceFileName !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32\DriverStore\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType, ServiceAccount
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SprySOCKS WIN_DRV / WIN_PLUS binary hash hit on Windows endpoint AIInstallation Medium
Detects execution or write of any of the 11 SHA1 hashes ESET attributes to SprySOCKS WIN_DRV and WIN_PLUS Windows variants. High-fidelity binary-match detection that flags both already-installed implants and fresh drops. Rationale: All 11 SHA1 hashes are pulled directly from the ESET article as confirmed SprySOCKS Windows variant samples. Hash equality is the highest-confidence detection shape — zero ambiguity on intent. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1033/
ATT&CKT1059 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandbox / malware analyst VM detonating the sample under controlled conditions
  • Threat-intel team intentionally pulling samples for YARA validation
  • Backup/forensics tools (FTK Imager, X-Ways) reading the binary while imaging an infected host's disk
  • Defender/AV file-scan event re-touching a quarantined sample
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("SANDBOX", "MALWARE", "FORENSIC", "-IR-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm hash via Defender DeviceFileEvents — record DeviceName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, AccountName. Differentiate execution (DeviceProcessEvents) vs dormant on-disk (DeviceFileEvents only). 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture memory + the binary, block the SHA1/SHA256 fleet-wide via Defender custom indicator. 3) Hunt: pivot on Vultr C2 IPs 207.148.78.36 / 207.148.75.122 across DeviceNetworkEvents for the last 90d; review DeviceLogonEvents on the infected host for the user account and check IdentityLogonEvents for lateral pivots; query DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities for CVE-2023-24932 exposure on the same host given possible UEFI bootkit chaining.

    "955BFC3DCC867256F9F46A606DEB0779FA3416D8",

    "D2C706B1EAF662BF0CE124B5032F73ED84BDA24A",
    "5F3B87CEF56683D9A9E19186E0FD0D8019B559C4",
    "C793CA31E3F6628B5C8986146953BF66232E9A30",
    "037DB2445F3D72388CB2CF8510563148E5A184BE"]);
union isfuzzy=true
    (DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(90d)

Boot Manager / BCD tampering indicative of CVE-2023-24932 BlackLotus-style UEFI bootkit AIInstallation Medium
ESET reports limited indications SprySOCKS deployment may chain a UEFI bootkit possibly exploiting CVE-2023-24932 (BlackLotus's Secure Boot bypass). Detects writes to the EFI System Partition boot manager and BCD modifications using bcdedit that are the on-disk signature of bootkit installation. Rationale: ESET explicitly notes possible CVE-2023-24932 (BlackLotus Secure Boot bypass) chaining. The canonical BlackLotus install signature is replacing bootmgfw.efi / bootx64.efi on the EFI system partition, or bcdedit modifying the bootmgr description / path. Excluding TrustedInstaller / MoUsoCoreWorker / setup.exe filters legitimate Windows Update boot manager refresh. Cross-checked against: • https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2023-24932 • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/bootkitty-analyzing-first-uefi-bootkit-linux/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1542/003/
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows Update KB5025885 / cumulative servicing pass refreshing boot manager outside TrustedInstaller wrapping
  • Dual-boot Linux installation writing to \EFI\Boot\bootx64.efi from a live USB
  • Disk-imaging restore (Veeam / Acronis bare-metal) rewriting EFI partition
  • Manual recovery — admin running bcdedit /set or bootrec /fixboot during repair
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe","MoUsoCoreWorker.exe","wuauclt.exe","setup.exe","bcdboot.exe","BootRec.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("services.exe","wininit.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull DeviceFileEvents to identify writing process + parent chain; collect the new .efi binary hash and verify Authenticode against Microsoft signer. Cross-check OS build vs KB5025885 / KB5036896 install state to rule out a real Windows Update servicing pass. 2) Contain: if signer is non-Microsoft or process chain is suspicious, image the disk before reboot (bootkit may persist across OS reinstall), isolate the host, escalate to IR for offline EFI analysis. 3) Hunt: query DeviceNetworkEvents for SprySOCKS C2 (207.148.78.36 / 207.148.75.122) from the same host; check DeviceProcessEvents for any of the 11 SprySOCKS SHA1s; pivot DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities for CVE-2023-24932 unpatched hosts across the fleet.
union isfuzzy=true
    (DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
        | where FolderPath has_any (@"\EFI\Microsoft\Boot\", @"\EFI\Boot\")
            or FileName in~ ("bootmgfw.efi", "bootmgr.efi", "bootx64.efi", "winload.efi")
        | where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe", "MoUsoCoreWorker.exe", "setup.exe", "BootRec.exe", "bcdboot.exe")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName),
    (DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
        | where FileName =~ "bcdedit.exe"
        | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/set", "/copy", "/create")
        | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("bootmgr", "path", "description", "{bootmgr}", "nointegritychecks", "testsigning")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType = "BcdeditExec", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256 = "", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine = ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName = AccountName)
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
    (ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\EFI\Microsoft\Boot\", @"\EFI\Boot\")
            or TargetFileName in~ ("bootmgfw.efi", "bootmgr.efi", "bootx64.efi", "winload.efi")
        | where ActingProcessName !has_any ("TrustedInstaller.exe", "MoUsoCoreWorker.exe", "setup.exe", "BootRec.exe", "bcdboot.exe")
        | project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, Event = "EfiFileWrite", File = TargetFileName, Path = TargetFilePath, Process = ActingProcessName, Cmd = ActingProcessCommandLine, User = ActorUsername),
    (ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where ActingProcessName =~ "bcdedit.exe" or TargetProcessName =~ "bcdedit.exe"
        | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/set", "/copy", "/create")
        | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bootmgr", "path", "description", "{bootmgr}", "nointegritychecks", "testsigning")
        | project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, Event = "BcdeditExec", File = ActingProcessName, Path = "", Process = ParentProcessName, Cmd = ActingProcessCommandLine, User = ActorUsername)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: EFI Boot Manager Tampering (Possible CVE-2023-24932 BlackLotus / SprySOCKS UEFI Chain)
id: 4a8b6c12-7e9d-43f5-bf21-9c8a7d3e4f01
description: Write to the EFI System Partition boot manager binaries by a process other than the legitimate Windows update / setup chain. Consistent with BlackLotus-style UEFI bootkit install possibly chained with SprySOCKS.
references:
    - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/fishmongers-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-windows/
    - https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2023-24932
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/17
tags:
    - attack.persistence
    - attack.defense_evasion
    - attack.t1542.003
logsource:
    category: file_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\EFI\Microsoft\Boot\'
            - '\EFI\Boot\'
    selection_name:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\bootmgfw.efi'
            - '\bootmgr.efi'
            - '\bootx64.efi'
            - '\winload.efi'
    filter_legit:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\TrustedInstaller.exe'
            - '\MoUsoCoreWorker.exe'
            - '\setup.exe'
            - '\BootRec.exe'
            - '\bcdboot.exe'
    condition: (selection_path or selection_name) and not filter_legit
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*\\EFI\\Microsoft\\Boot\\* OR *\\efi\\microsoft\\boot\\* OR *\\EFI\\Boot\\*) OR @TargetFilename:(*\\bootmgfw.efi OR *\\bootmgr.efi OR *\\bootx64.efi OR *\\winload.efi)) -@Image:(*\\TrustedInstaller.exe OR *\\MoUsoCoreWorker.exe OR *\\setup.exe OR *\\BootRec.exe OR *\\bcdboot.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| regex("(?i)\\\\(EFI\\\\Microsoft\\\\Boot\\\\|EFI\\\\Boot\\\\|bootmgfw\\.efi|bootmgr\\.efi|bootx64\\.efi|winload\\.efi)", field=TargetFileName)
| NOT regex("(?i)\\\\(TrustedInstaller|MoUsoCoreWorker|setup|BootRec|bcdboot)\\.exe", field=ContextImageFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-24932")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-24932")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,

Fake Microsoft Alerts Used to Deploy North Korean NarwhalRAT Malware

The Hacker News
2026-06-16 16 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ScarCruft fake Microsoft Account 'OTP abuse' alert with ZIP attachment · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] NarwhalRAT in-memory loader: python.exe processing a Windows CAT file · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] LNK from extracted ZIP spawning batch script that downloads Python and CAT file · [LLM] Scheduled task creation with NarwhalRAT 'Microsoft*TaskMachine' naming convention · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] NarwhalRAT C2 to daehoat.com / novel21.co.kr / pCloud dead-drop with folderid+auth · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] NarwhalRAT staging directory %APPDATA%\naverwhale (Naver Whale browser masquerade) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
ScarCruft fake Microsoft Account 'OTP abuse' alert with ZIP attachment AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound spear-phishing emails impersonating Microsoft Account security notifications about repeated OTP generation / abnormal activity, with a ZIP attachment that conceals a malicious LNK file. This is the article-specific NarwhalRAT initial-access lure. Rationale: Uses article's exact lure pattern (impersonated MS Account security alert about repeated OTP generation / abnormal activity) combined with the specific ZIP-containing-LNK delivery shape. Genians' report is the primary source; no second source needed because IOCs were taken directly from the named research org. Sentinel left empty because the listed Sentinel tenant schema in this prompt does not include EmailEvents / EmailAttachmentInfo — inbound mail phishing visibility for this tenant is Defender XDR only. Cross-checked against: • https://www.genians.co.kr/en/blog/threat_intelligence/narwhal-rat
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1598.003
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Microsoft account security notifications spoofed via lookalike domains used in phishing tests
  • Internal IT security awareness training emails containing simulated MS-account lures
  • Bug bounty / external researcher submissions referencing OTP abuse in subject line
  • Third-party SSO partners sending password-rotation reminders that mention 'Microsoft account'
Suppression filter
| where not(SenderFromAddress in~ ("security-noreply@microsoft.com", "account-security-noreply@accountprotection.microsoft.com")) and not(Subject has "phishing simulation")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the EmailAttachmentInfo SHA256 of the ZIP and any LNK contained within; check VirusTotal and abuse.ch for the hash; pivot on RecipientEmailAddress to confirm whether the recipient opened the attachment (DeviceFileEvents extraction of the LNK; DeviceProcessEvents for explorer.exe spawning cmd/powershell shortly after). 2) Contain: block SenderFromAddress and SenderFromDomain at the connector; recall the message tenant-wide via Quarantine and Soft Delete; isolate any device that extracted the LNK. 3) Hunt: across the tenant, look for any inbound mail in the last 30 days from the same sender domain, any other recipients of the same SHA256 attachment, and downstream IOCs (process tree from LNK execution, connections to daehoat.com / novel21.co.kr, scheduled tasks named 'MicrosoftUserInterfacePicturesUpdateTackMachine' or 'MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackageTaskMachine').
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| where Subject has_any ("Microsoft account", "security alert", "OTP", "one-time password", "abnormal activity", "password")
| where not(SenderFromDomain endswith "microsoft.com") and not(SenderMailFromDomain endswith "microsoft.com")
| join kind=inner (
    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName endswith ".zip"
    | project NetworkMessageId, AttachmentName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256, FileSize
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, AttachmentName, AttachmentSHA256, FileSize
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| where Subject has_any ("Microsoft account", "security alert", "OTP", "one-time password", "abnormal activity", "password")
| where not(SenderFromDomain endswith "microsoft.com") and not(SenderMailFromDomain endswith "microsoft.com")
| join kind=inner (
    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where FileName endswith ".zip"
    | project NetworkMessageId, AttachmentName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256, FileSize
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, AttachmentName, AttachmentSHA256, FileSize
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Inbound Microsoft Account Security Alert Lure with ZIP Attachment
id: 5b0e8e8c-6d5b-4c2d-9e2c-2c1d8e8f5a01
description: Detects ScarCruft NarwhalRAT delivery pattern - email impersonating Microsoft Account security alert with ZIP attachment that contains a LNK file.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/fake-microsoft-alerts-used-to-deploy.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1566.001
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: email
  product: microsoft365
detection:
  selection_subject:
    Subject|contains:
      - 'Microsoft account'
      - 'security alert'
      - 'OTP'
      - 'one-time password'
      - 'abnormal activity'
  selection_attachment:
    AttachmentName|endswith: '.zip'
  filter_legit:
    SenderFromDomain|endswith: 'microsoft.com'
  condition: all of selection_* and not filter_legit
level: high
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where All_Email.action="delivered" All_Email.file_name="*.zip" (All_Email.subject="*Microsoft account*" OR All_Email.subject="*security alert*" OR All_Email.subject="*OTP*" OR All_Email.subject="*one-time password*" OR All_Email.subject="*abnormal activity*") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject All_Email.file_name All_Email.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | where NOT match(src_user, "(?i)@microsoft\.com$") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where All_Email.action="delivered" All_Email.file_name="*.zip" (All_Email.subject="*Microsoft account*" OR All_Email.subject="*security alert*" OR All_Email.subject="*OTP*" OR All_Email.subject="*one-time password*" OR All_Email.subject="*abnormal activity*") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject All_Email.file_name All_Email.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | where NOT match(src_user, "(?i)@microsoft\.com$") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
LNK from extracted ZIP spawning batch script that downloads Python and CAT file AIInstallation High
Detects the NarwhalRAT loader chain: an LNK file (extracted from a phishing ZIP) launches cmd.exe to run a batch script that uses curl/bitsadmin/powershell to fetch the legitimate Python installer plus a malicious Windows security catalog (.cat) file from attacker infrastructure. Rationale: Article explicitly describes the chain LNK -> batch script -> downloads Python + CAT file. Combines explorer.exe-spawned shell parent (the only way an extracted-from-ZIP LNK can launch) with downloader keywords and article's exact second-stage indicators (.cat, Python download). Cross-referenced with Genians GSC public IOC bundle. Cross-checked against: • https://www.genians.co.kr/en/blog/threat_intelligence/narwhal-rat
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin running ad-hoc cmd.exe scripts from a desktop shortcut that uses curl for legitimate downloads
  • Developer LNK shortcuts to .bat build scripts that call python.exe
  • Software installer LNKs that invoke bitsadmin for first-run updates
  • Help-desk troubleshooting LNKs that invoke Invoke-WebRequest to fetch diagnostic tooling
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("sccm", "intune", "chocolatey", "winget")) and not(AccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the LNK target via DeviceFileEvents (look for InitiatingProcessFileName='explorer.exe' and FileName endswith '.lnk' within minutes prior); pull SHA256 and check against IOC list (3715092a..., 7cef19f9..., 7eb9cee1..., b6b06023...). 2) Contain: isolate the device via Defender Live Response; kill the cmd/powershell tree and any python.exe child; remove the scheduled task if already created. 3) Hunt: pivot on the parent ZIP - find EmailAttachmentInfo for the SHA256 of the ZIP, identify all recipients tenant-wide, look for the staging folder %APPDATA%\naverwhale, look for outbound connections to daehoat.com, novel21.co.kr, fe01.co.kr, and the IPs 121.254.222.10/80, 211.239.157.126, 218.150.78.198/231, 61.100.9.206.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".lnk", ".bat")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl", "bitsadmin", "Invoke-WebRequest", "python", ".cat", "daehoat", "novel21", "fe01.co.kr")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "explorer.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "cmd.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "pwsh.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "cscript.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any (".lnk", ".bat") or CommandLine has_any ("curl", "bitsadmin", "Invoke-WebRequest", "python", ".cat", "daehoat", "novel21", "fe01.co.kr")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: LNK Extracted From Phishing ZIP Spawns Loader Batch Script
id: 7e4d3a9c-1f2b-4a8e-9c11-3a5b1c2d8f02
description: Detects NarwhalRAT loader chain where explorer.exe-spawned cmd/powershell from an LNK invokes curl/bitsadmin/python plus a .cat fetch.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/fake-microsoft-alerts-used-to-deploy.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.t1059.003
  - attack.execution
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\explorer.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
  selection_indicators:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '.lnk'
      - '.bat'
      - 'curl'
      - 'bitsadmin'
      - 'Invoke-WebRequest'
      - 'python'
      - '.cat'
      - 'daehoat'
      - 'novel21'
      - 'fe01.co.kr'
  condition: all of selection_*
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\explorer.exe OR *\Explorer.exe OR *\EXPLORER.EXE) @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\wscript.exe OR *\cscript.exe) @CommandLine:(*lnk* OR *bat* OR *curl* OR *bitsadmin* OR *Invoke-WebRequest* OR *python* OR *.cat* OR *daehoat* OR *novel21* OR *fe01.co.kr*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/explorer\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/(cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)(\\.lnk|\\.bat|curl|bitsadmin|Invoke-WebRequest|python|\\.cat|daehoat|novel21|fe01\\.co\\.kr)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="explorer.exe" Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") (Processes.parent_process="*.lnk*" OR Processes.process="*.lnk*" OR Processes.process="*.bat*") (Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*bitsadmin*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-WebRequest*" OR Processes.process="*python*" OR Processes.process="*.cat*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="explorer.exe" Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") (Processes.parent_process="*.lnk*" OR Processes.process="*.lnk*" OR Processes.process="*.bat*") (Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*bitsadmin*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-WebRequest*" OR Processes.process="*python*" OR Processes.process="*.cat*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Scheduled task creation with NarwhalRAT 'Microsoft*TaskMachine' naming convention AIInstallation High
Detects creation of scheduled tasks whose names follow the ScarCruft NarwhalRAT convention: 'MicrosoftUserInterfacePicturesUpdateTackMachine' or 'MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackageTaskMachine'. Naming convention shared across multiple Python-based ScarCruft campaigns - tasks launch the CAT file that pulls and in-memory loads the main payload. Rationale: Article gives two literal task names ('MicrosoftUserInterfacePicturesUpdateTackMachine', 'MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackageTaskMachine'); both are distinct enough that combined with schtasks.exe /create they are near zero-FP. Note 'TackMachine' is not a typo - the article explicitly preserves that naming. Also checks the on-disk task XML drop in %WINDIR%\System32\Tasks\ as a second pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://www.genians.co.kr/en/blog/threat_intelligence/narwhal-rat
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager (MECM/SCCM) deploying scheduled tasks with 'Microsoft' prefixes via custom packages
  • Microsoft Office click-to-run telemetry tasks created during MSI install
  • Internal IT scripted task creation using 'MicrosoftUpdates' or similar prefix conventions
  • Windows Update Medic Service (WaaSMedicSvc) creating Microsoft-prefixed remediation tasks
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe", "tiworker.exe", "officeclicktorun.exe", "setup.exe", "msiexec.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the XML body of the matching task from %WINDIR%\System32\Tasks\<name> via Defender Live Response; identify the action (typically launches the .cat file via cmd or powershell). 2) Contain: delete the scheduled task (schtasks /delete /tn <name> /f), kill any running children, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: across the estate look for any other Microsoft-prefixed tasks created in the same 7-day window from non-MECM parents; pivot on InitiatingProcessFileName to find the loader; look for in-memory python.exe processes and outbound traffic to article IOCs (daehoat.com, novel21.co.kr, pCloud).
union
(
  DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
  | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("MicrosoftUserInterfacePictures", "MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackage", "TaskMachine", "TackMachine")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
),
(
  DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where FolderPath has @"\System32\Tasks\"
  | where FileName has_any ("MicrosoftUserInterfacePictures", "MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackage", "TaskMachine", "TackMachine")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
)
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(
  SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where NewProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe"
  | where CommandLine has "/create"
  | where CommandLine has_any ("MicrosoftUserInterfacePictures", "MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackage", "TaskMachine", "TackMachine")
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
),
(
  SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where EventID == 4698
  | where EventData has_any ("MicrosoftUserInterfacePictures", "MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackage", "TaskMachine", "TackMachine")
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, EventID, EventData
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ScarCruft NarwhalRAT Scheduled Task Naming Pattern
id: a1f7b2d8-9c4e-4e8b-bf01-3d2c8a9b5e03
description: Detects creation of scheduled task with the ScarCruft NarwhalRAT naming convention (MicrosoftUserInterfacePicturesUpdateTackMachine, MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackageTaskMachine).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/fake-microsoft-alerts-used-to-deploy.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_bin:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
  selection_create:
    CommandLine|contains: '/create'
  selection_name:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'MicrosoftUserInterfacePictures'
      - 'MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackage'
      - 'TaskMachine'
      - 'TackMachine'
  condition: all of selection_*
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\schtasks.exe OR *\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:(*\/create* AND (*MicrosoftUserInterfacePictures* OR *MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackage* OR *TaskMachine* OR *TackMachine*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/schtasks\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)\\/create", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(?i)(MicrosoftUserInterfacePictures|MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackage|TaskMachine|TackMachine)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" Processes.process="*/create*" (Processes.process="*Microsoft*TaskMachine*" OR Processes.process="*Microsoft*TackMachine*" OR Processes.process="*MicrosoftUserInterfacePictures*" OR Processes.process="*MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackage*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" Processes.process="*/create*" (Processes.process="*Microsoft*TaskMachine*" OR Processes.process="*Microsoft*TackMachine*" OR Processes.process="*MicrosoftUserInterfacePictures*" OR Processes.process="*MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackage*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
NarwhalRAT in-memory loader: python.exe processing a Windows CAT file AIExploitation High
Detects the article-specific in-memory execution structure where the legitimate Python interpreter (downloaded from python.org) is launched with a Windows security catalog (.cat) file as input - the CAT is repurposed as a Python script container so the main payload runs in memory without disk artifacts. Rationale: Article: 'launch the CAT file responsible for fetching and running the main payload in memory without leaving any artifacts on disk' and 'Python-based multi-stage loader, an in-memory execution structure'. Combination python.exe + .cat extension is anomalous (CAT files are normally consumed by Windows code signing / WinVerifyTrust, not Python). Very rare benign hits. Cross-checked against: • https://www.genians.co.kr/en/blog/threat_intelligence/narwhal-rat
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1027 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Python developers genuinely processing certificate trust list files for code-signing tooling research
  • Antivirus signature-development workflow scripts that diff catalog files
  • Internal red-team education modules demonstrating LOLBin script abuse
  • Custom Microsoft Update validation tooling that wraps signtool/makecat with python wrappers
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\Common Files\microsoft shared", @"\Windows\System32\CatRoot"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the .cat path - if it sits in %APPDATA%, %TEMP%, %PUBLIC%, or %APPDATA%\naverwhale this is highly likely malicious; pull the file hash and content sample via Defender Live Response. 2) Contain: kill the python.exe tree, isolate host, capture memory dump for IR. 3) Hunt: pivot DeviceNetworkEvents on the same python.exe ProcessId to find C2 (daehoat.com, novel21.co.kr, pCloud); look for the scheduled task that launched the chain; sweep estate for any other python.exe + .cat combinations in the last 30 days.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "python.exe" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "python.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".cat" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ".cat"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "python.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "python.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".cat"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

id: 8b3c9f1a-6d2e-4a5c-9012-4e6d2f3a8b04

NarwhalRAT staging directory %APPDATA%\naverwhale (Naver Whale browser masquerade) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects creation, write, or process activity referencing the article's distinctive staging directory %APPDATA%\naverwhale, which NarwhalRAT uses to stage harvested keylogger output, screenshots, audio recordings, and USB media before exfil. Name masquerades as the South Korean Naver Whale browser. Rationale: Article explicitly: 'The moniker NarwhalRAT is a reference to the malware's use of %APPDATA%\naverwhale to stage the harvested information' and the name masquerades as Naver Whale. Path string is unique enough to be near-zero FP because the legitimate Naver Whale browser uses '%LOCALAPPDATA%\Naver\Naver Whale' (different parent, different casing, space, different folder) - the 'naverwhale' (one word, no space, in Roaming) is the article's distinctive IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.genians.co.kr/en/blog/threat_intelligence/narwhal-rat
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1074.001 T1056.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Korean-speaking developers writing tooling that programmatically references a folder literally called 'naverwhale' for legitimate research
  • Naver Whale browser uninstaller leaving residual breadcrumbs under Roaming during cleanup
  • Internal threat-intel team running detonation/IOC validation against the article's path on a sandbox machine
  • Security researchers writing test cases that drop files into the same path
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("whale.exe", "naver_whale.exe", "WhaleUpdate.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate contents of %APPDATA%\naverwhale via Live Response - expect keylog dumps, screenshots, audio captures; pull file metadata. 2) Contain: isolate device, kill python.exe process(es) writing to the path, snapshot the folder before purging for forensic preservation. 3) Hunt: across all hosts grep DeviceFileEvents for any FolderPath has 'naverwhale'; pivot the writing process backwards through process tree to confirm Python loader chain; check DeviceNetworkEvents for exfil to daehoat.com, novel21.co.kr, pCloud API endpoints.
union
(
  DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Roaming\naverwhale"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
),
(
  DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has @"\AppData\Roaming\naverwhale" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has @"\AppData\Roaming\naverwhale"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ActionType="ProcessRef", FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\AppData\Roaming\naverwhale"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:

logsource:

| regex("(?i)\\\\AppData\\\\Roaming\\\\naverwhale", field=TargetFileName)

ENDPOINT

NarwhalRAT C2 to daehoat.com / novel21.co.kr / pCloud dead-drop with folderid+auth AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound C2 traffic to ScarCruft NarwhalRAT primary relays (daehoat.com, novel21.co.kr) and secondary pCloud-based dead-drop resolver - identifies pCloud abuse via the article-specific URL parameter combination 'folderid' + 'auth' which the malware uses to fetch staged commands. Rationale: Article names two primary C2 relays ('daehoat[.]com' and 'novel21[.]co.kr') plus the pCloud API dead-drop resolver pattern with folderid+auth params; pre-extracted IOC bundle adds three more Korean-hosted domains and six IPs. Multiple-table union covers EDR network telemetry plus proxy/firewall (CEF/CommonSecurityLog) and DNS — common SOC visibility gaps in different orgs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.genians.co.kr/en/blog/threat_intelligence/narwhal-rat • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.001 T1090.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Korean-speaking employees legitimately browsing daehoat.com (a real Korean-hosted site) or novel21.co.kr literary websites
  • Backup/sync clients of pCloud users in the org transferring folderid+auth normally — normal pCloud client UI does use those params
  • Threat-intel team detonating samples in production network without isolation
  • Public proxy / Tor exit nodes that happen to share one of the listed IPs
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pcloud.exe", "pcloud-sync.exe", "chrome.exe", "msedge.exe", "firefox.exe", "whale.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot DeviceNetworkEvents on InitiatingProcessFileName - if python.exe or schtasks-spawned cmd.exe is the initiator on a non-Korea-business host, escalate to incident; check whether the device also shows %APPDATA%\naverwhale. 2) Contain: block IPs and domains at perimeter and EDR network containment; isolate the host; capture memory. 3) Hunt: 30-day backtrack across all hosts for any of the six listed IPs and five domains; check Email egress for any messages to recipients matching the same actor pattern; for pCloud, look for any other python.exe processes making pCloud API calls with folderid+auth - those are the dead-drop fetch routines.
union
(
  DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteUrl has_any ("daehoat.com", "novel21.co.kr", "fe01.co.kr", "crwellfood.com", "webhostingkorea.com")
     or RemoteIP in ("121.254.222.10", "121.254.222.80", "211.239.157.126", "218.150.78.198", "218.150.78.231", "61.100.9.206")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
),
(

  | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "python.exe" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("folderid", "naverwhale")

)
| order by Timestamp desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
